newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing announces new Business Jet sales.
newsitem.headline: Boeing announces new Business Jet sales.

text.p: U.S. aircraft giant Boeing Co muscled into the corporate jet market on Saturday with further sales of its plush new Business Jet and plans to increase launch production next year.

The company said at the week-long Paris airshow which opened today that it sold two more Business Jets last week, priced at $30.5 million apiece before fitting out, taking its tally of orders to 20 aircraft from 18 customers since its launch last year.
The company said buyers so far include blue-chip Fortune 100 corporations, heads of state and wealthy individuals, such as champion golfer Greg Norman, who signed up last week.
As a result, the company said it has decided to produce nine of the aircraft next year instead of the four originally planned, and 24 aircraft in 1999, up from the six to eight previously envisaged.

"Right now, we have committed production for nine airplanes in the fourth quarter of 1998 and 24, or two a month, in 1999," Boeing Business Jets president Borge Boeskov told a news conference. "This is a tremendous increase in the production rate from where we originally thought this thing was going to be," he said.

Boeing launched the new jet, a special hybrid development of its 737-700 and 737-800 commercial airliners, to grab sales at the top end of the corporate jet business from Gulfstream's sleek new Gulfstream V and rival Canadian firm Bombardier's Global Express long-range jets.

Boeskov said this niche market was small compared to Boeing's multi-billion dollar business making over 500 airliners a year, but the move promised not only extra profits, since development cost "tens of millions," instead of several billions of dollars for a new airliner, but also prestige.
"You may not think it is a big deal but it is in many ways because this is a new market for Boeing, it's a new extension of our market domain," Boeskov said.
"We also will get to know a whole new set of people -- very important corporations, very important individual people and...heads of state who will be flying these airplanes."

Boeskov declined to say how many Business Jets needed to be sold to break-even but he warned that prices were rising, to $32 million from next month to include some additional equipment, with a further increase expected next year.
"We will probably raise the price again some time early next year...we just want to get the price up there a little more."
